original_question: Do there exist Seidel matrices of order at least 14 with exactly three distinct eigenvalues whose switching class contains no regular graph?
target_in_paper: Problem 3.33 in Section 3.8: "Do there exist any Seidel matrices of order at least 14 with precisely three distinct eigenvalues whose switching class does not contain a regular graph?"
correct_elements: Your draft already matches the paper's target almost verbatim. It has the correct existential form, the correct order threshold (at least 14), the correct spectral condition (exactly/precisely three distinct eigenvalues), and the correct obstruction (the switching class contains no regular graph).
missing_details: State what a Seidel matrix is: for a finite simple undirected graph G on n vertices, S(G) = J_n - I_n - 2A(G), a real symmetric n x n matrix with 0 diagonal and off-diagonal entries in {+1, -1}.
Make explicit that the switching class is the Seidel-switching class of the graph underlying the Seidel matrix.
If desired for full stand-alone precision, define switching equivalently by S(H) = D S(G) D for some diagonal matrix D with diagonal entries in {+1, -1}.
Clarify that 'regular graph' means an ordinary unsigned d-regular graph for some integer d.
Tie the matrix language to graph language: a Seidel matrix is attached to a simple graph G, and the switching class is a class of graphs rather than an abstract class of matrices.
refined_question: Does there exist a finite simple graph G on n >= 14 vertices such that its Seidel matrix S(G) = J_n - I_n - 2A(G) has exactly three distinct eigenvalues, but no graph H in the Seidel-switching class of G (equivalently, no H with S(H) = D S(G) D for some diagonal D with entries +/-1) is regular?
justification: The draft is targeting Problem 3.33, not the neighboring Problem 3.34. Section 3.8 first defines Seidel matrices and identifies switching of the associated signed complete graph with Seidel switching. The paper then states Problem 3.33 in essentially the same words as your draft. The nearby context explains why this exact formulation is sharp: order bounds matter because Seidel matrices with exactly three distinct eigenvalues were classified for order less than 23, Greaves found only one example up to order 12 whose switching class contains no regular graph, and if one of the three eigenvalues is simple then the switching class contains a strongly regular graph. So the faithful stand-alone rewrite should preserve the existential question, the threshold n >= 14, the condition of exactly three distinct eigenvalues, and the absence of any regular graph in the Seidel-switching class, while only adding the definitions of Seidel matrix and switching class.
